chapter.name: Statistics
chapter.blurb: This chapter moves from measures of central tendency to measures of dispersion, which describe how scattered the data are. It covers the range, the mean deviation about the mean and about the median for ungrouped, discrete and continuous data, and the variance and standard deviation, including the shortcut (step-deviation) method. It ends with problems on how the mean and variance respond when every observation is changed or a wrong observation is corrected.

scope_in.item: Recall the mean and the median (odd and even number of observations) and explain, with two series having equal mean and median, why a measure of central tendency alone is not sufficient and a measure of dispersion is needed

Name the measures of dispersion (range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, standard deviation) and find the range as maximum value minus minimum value, noting that it gives only a rough idea of scatter
Explain why the sum of deviations from the mean is zero and define mean deviation about a central value a as the mean of the absolute values of the deviations
Calculate the mean deviation about the mean and about the median for ungrouped data, arranging the data in order to find the median
Calculate the mean deviation about the mean for a discrete frequency distribution using N = Sum f, mean = Sum f x / N and (1/N) Sum f |x - mean|
Find the median of a discrete frequency distribution from cumulative frequencies and calculate the mean deviation about the median
Calculate the mean deviation about the mean for a continuous frequency distribution using class mid-points, finding the mean directly or by the step-deviation method a + (Sum f d / N) * h

Find the median of a continuous frequency distribution from the median class with l + ((N/2 - C)/f) * h and calculate the mean deviation about the median using mid-points; make inclusive classes continuous by moving each limit by 0.5 where an exercise hint asks for it

State the limitations of mean deviation (median unrepresentative when variability is very high, mean deviation about the mean not very scientific, absolute values not open to further algebraic treatment)

Explain why the sum of squared deviations is not a proper measure and define variance as the mean of the squares of the deviations from the mean and standard deviation as its positive square root; calculate both for ungrouped data, including through Sum x^2 / n - (mean)^2

Calculate the variance and standard deviation of a discrete frequency distribution and of a continuous frequency distribution (through mid-points), using (1/N) Sum f (x - mean)^2 or (1/N^2)[N Sum f x^2 - (Sum f x)^2]
Use the shortcut (step-deviation) method y = (x - A)/h: mean = A + h * (mean of y), variance of x = h^2 * variance of y, sigma = (h/N) sqrt(N Sum f y^2 - (Sum f y)^2)
Use the facts that multiplying every observation by k multiplies the mean by k and the variance by k^2, and that adding a constant to every observation leaves the variance unchanged
Find two missing observations from a given mean and variance, and correct a mean and standard deviation after a wrongly recorded observation is replaced or omitted

concepts.name: Measures of dispersion and range
concepts.description: Why a measure of central tendency is not enough, what a measure of dispersion is, and the range as maximum value minus minimum value, with its limitation.
concepts.idea: Two sets of data can share the same mean and median and still be scattered very differently, so a single number describing the variability is needed alongside the average.
concepts.rule: Range = maximum value - minimum value. The measures of dispersion are range, quartile deviation, mean deviation and standard deviation (quartile deviation is not studied here). The range gives only a rough idea of scatter and says nothing about dispersion from a central value. Median: arrange the data in order; for odd n it is the ((n + 1)/2)th observation, for even n the mean of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th observations.
concepts.example: Batsman A scores from 0 to 117 (range 117) and batsman B from 46 to 60 (range 14); both have mean 53 and median 53, but B is far more consistent.

concepts.name: Mean deviation for ungrouped data
concepts.description: Mean deviation about the mean and about the median for a list of observations, as the mean of the absolute values of the deviations.
concepts.idea: Deviations from the mean always add up to zero, so we drop their signs and average the distances of the observations from the central value.
concepts.rule: M.D.(a) = (sum of the absolute values of the deviations from a)/(number of observations). M.D. about the mean = (1/n) * Sum |x - mean|; M.D. about the median = (1/n) * Sum |x - M|, where M is the median of the data arranged in order.
concepts.example: For 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 4, 8, 12 the mean is 9, the absolute deviations are 3, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 1, 3 (sum 22), so M.D. about the mean = 22/8 = 2.75.

concepts.name: Mean deviation for a discrete frequency distribution
concepts.description: Mean deviation about the mean and about the median when values x occur with frequencies f, including finding the median from cumulative frequencies.
concepts.idea: Each absolute deviation is counted as many times as its value occurs, so it is weighted by the frequency before averaging over N.
concepts.rule: N = Sum f; mean = (Sum f x)/N; M.D. about the mean = (1/N) * Sum f |x - mean|. The median is the observation whose cumulative frequency is equal to or just greater than N/2; M.D. about the median = (1/N) * Sum f |x - M|.

concepts.name: Mean deviation for a continuous frequency distribution
concepts.description: Mean deviation about the mean and about the median for class-interval data using class mid-points, the step-deviation method for the mean, the median-class formula, and the limitations of mean deviation.
concepts.idea: Each class is treated as if all its frequency sat at the mid-point, after which the work is the same as for a discrete frequency distribution.
concepts.rule: Use mid-points x. Mean by step-deviation: mean = a + (Sum f d / N) * h with d = (x - a)/h. Median = l + ((N/2 - C)/f) * h, where l, f, h are the lower limit, frequency and width of the median class and C is the cumulative frequency of the class just before it. M.D. = (1/N) * Sum f |x - mean| or (1/N) * Sum f |x - M|.
concepts.example: Classes 10-20, ..., 70-80 with frequencies 2, 3, 8, 14, 8, 3, 2 have mean 45 and Sum f |x - 45| = 400, so M.D. about the mean = 400/40 = 10.

concepts.name: Variance and standard deviation of ungrouped data
concepts.description: Variance as the mean of the squares of the deviations from the mean, and standard deviation as its positive square root, for a list of observations.
concepts.idea: Squaring the deviations removes their signs; dividing the sum of squares by the number of observations makes sets of different sizes comparable.
concepts.rule: Variance sigma^2 = (1/n) * Sum (x - mean)^2; standard deviation sigma = sqrt(variance). Equivalently sigma^2 = (Sum x^2)/n - (mean)^2. The standard deviation has the same unit as the observations.
concepts.example: For 6, 8, 10, ..., 24 (ten observations) the mean is 15 and Sum (x - 15)^2 = 330, so the variance is 33 and the standard deviation is sqrt(33), about 5.74.

concepts.name: Variance and standard deviation of frequency distributions
concepts.description: Variance and standard deviation of discrete and continuous frequency distributions, the formula using Sum f x^2, and the shortcut (step-deviation) method.
concepts.idea: Squared deviations are weighted by frequency; classes are replaced by mid-points; large values are shrunk by shifting to an assumed mean A and scaling by h.
concepts.rule: sigma^2 = (1/N) * Sum f (x - mean)^2 = (1/N^2) * [N * Sum f x^2 - (Sum f x)^2]. Shortcut: y = (x - A)/h, mean = A + h * (Sum f y)/N, sigma^2 = (h^2/N^2) * [N * Sum f y^2 - (Sum f y)^2], so sigma(x) = h * sigma(y).
concepts.example: Classes 30-40, ..., 90-100 with frequencies 3, 7, 12, 15, 8, 3, 2: with A = 65, h = 10, Sum f y = -15 and Sum f y^2 = 105, so mean = 62, variance = (100/2500)(5250 - 225) = 201.

concepts.name: Effect of changing the observations on mean and variance
concepts.description: How the mean, variance and standard deviation change when every observation is multiplied by a constant or increased by a constant, finding missing observations from a given mean and variance, and correcting a mean and standard deviation after a wrongly recorded observation.
concepts.idea: Adding a constant shifts every observation and the mean together, so deviations do not change; multiplying by k stretches every deviation by k, so squared deviations grow by k^2.
concepts.rule: If each observation is multiplied by k, the mean becomes k times and the variance k^2 times the original. If a is added to each observation, the mean increases by a and the variance is unchanged. Sum x = n * mean and Sum x^2 = n * (variance + mean^2) let a wrong observation be removed and the right one put in.
concepts.example: The variance of 20 observations is 5; if each observation is multiplied by 2 the new variance is 2^2 * 5 = 20.
